column3: The Hebrew describes being advanced in days and says he did not become warm, without a separate verb for ability.
The Hebrew uses an unnamed plural subject for searching, calls the king “my lord,” and says she will lie “in your bosom”; BSB uses “Let us,” “our lord,” and “by his side.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew describes her as very beautiful, without a superlative, and says the king did not “know” her; BSB has “unsurpassed” and “had no relations.”
The Hebrew calls him Haggith’s son without explicitly naming David and uses singular “chariot”; BSB has plural “chariots.”
The Hebrew asks why he has acted thus and describes a woman bearing him after Absalom; BSB uses present “act” and passive “born.”
The Hebrew leaves the subject unnamed; BSB supplies Adonijah.
The Hebrew says they “were not with” Adonijah; BSB expresses this as refusing to join him.
The Hebrew calls the invited brothers “sons of the king” and names fattened animals without specifying calves.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats the advising root in verb and noun and calls both lives “soul.”
The Hebrew has two movement commands, “go and enter,” without a separate “at once.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew coordinates the king’s age and the service with “and”; BSB introduces an explicit “Since” relation.
The Hebrew names the king again as questioner and asks “What is to you?”; BSB uses “who” and “What is your desire?”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats “now.”
The Hebrew has no separate “other” in the invitation to all the king’s sons.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says they will be “sinners”; BSB has “counted as criminals.”
The Hebrew leaves Bathsheba unnamed; BSB supplies her name.
The Hebrew reports the announcement actively with unnamed people and leaves the entering man unnamed; BSB uses passive reporting and supplies Nathan.
Close to the Hebrew.

Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew asks whether the matter came from the king and separately says he did not inform his servant.
The Hebrew introduces the king’s words with answering and speaking and repeats “the king”; BSB condenses the introduction and uses “him” in the last clause.
